To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a novel test criterion called Surprise Adequancy, and show that it can be effectively used to improve classification accuracy of deep neural networks against adversarial examples.
we propose and implement a new coverage criterion, called Surprise Adecuacy for Deep Learning (SADL).

(i) SADL is an effective and fine grained test adequacy criterion that is able to guide systematic sampling of inputs that are sufficiently but not overt surprising to training data, and that (ii) such systematic sampling can improve DL system’s accuracy against adversarial inputs by up to 75.6% via retraining.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and evaluating novel testing approaches that can systematically guide the search for adversarial examples in DL systems, which can subsequently be used for improving their robustness.
the development of a novel coverage criterion for testing of deep learning systems, and its evaluation for guiding testing of deep learning-based safety-critical applications.
guiding the testing of DL systems using a fine-grained coverage criterion based on the behaviour exhibited by DL systems with respect their training data.

SADL is an effective and novel approach for the testing of Deep Learning Systems.
SADL provides a novel and effective test adequacy criterion that is based on the surprise of an execution of a DL model with respect to its training data.
the proposed criterion can be used as a test oracle for testing DL systems and can be used to guide retraining of DL systems to make them more robust to adversarial examples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SADL can be used to guide testing of DL systems to improve their robustness against adversarial examples.
SADL provides a novel and practical test adequacy criterion to guide the testing of DL systems and can be used to improve the robustness of DL systems against attacks.
SADL can be used to guide systematic testing of DL systems and to improve their robustness against adversarial examples.

surprise can be used as an adequacy criteria to guide testing of DL systems to improve their robustness.
the behaviour of a DL system with respect to its training data is a good indicator of the correctness of a DL system, and can be used as a basis for test adequacy criterion.
surprise of inputs can be used as an indicator of the robustness of DL systems.
